extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; economists and policymakers interested in classical price theory
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and classification of how different kinds of 'rude produce' (agricultural and natural products) have their prices affected by the progress of improvement, cultivation, and wealth. The text explains mechanisms (supply elasticity, perishability, market extent, production costs) that determine whether and how prices rise or fall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precious metals flow to rich countries because of higher prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Gold and silver naturally resort to a rich country not because they are cheaper there but because they are dearer — a superiority of price attracts them; when that superiority ceases, they stop flowing there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to luxury goods and curiosities: precious metals follow superior price. This rejects the idea that increased precious metals from growing wealth diminishes their value; instead, they are drawn by higher nominal prices in prosperous countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominal price rises reflect rises in real price, not degradation of money
rubrics_metrics.description: When many kinds of produce come to exchange for a greater quantity of silver, it is not because silver has become cheaper but because those commodities have become really dearer — i.e., their real price (the labour and subsistence they command) has risen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish nominal (money) price from real price (labour/commodities). Rising nominal prices during improvement signal increased real value of commodities due to increased labour/subsistence costs in producing/bringing them to market.

rubrics_metrics.name: First sort of produce — essentially unmultipliable by industry: prices can rise without bound
rubrics_metrics.description: Commodities which nature produces only in certain limited quantities and which are very perishable (rare birds, fishes, many kinds of game, migratory birds) cannot be multiplied by human industry; with rising wealth/demand their price may rise to any degree of extravagance and seems not to have a certain boundary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because supply cannot increase in response to higher demand, competition among buyers can drive prices arbitrarily high. Historical examples (Roman prices for rare birds and fish) illustrate that high nominal prices reflected very high real costs/values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second sort of produce — can be multiplied in proportion to demand: prices rise but are bounded
rubrics_metrics.description: Products which human industry can multiply proportionally to demand (useful cultivated plants and animals that replace wild abundances) have prices that rise during improvement, but converge to a boundary — the price at which it becomes as profitable to cultivate land for them as for other uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: as price rises, more land and labor are devoted to producing them (e.g., turning tillage to pasture or cultivating feed), so supply increases until profitability equalizes. Examples include cattle, poultry, dairy, hogs. Local factors (manure availability, stock, farmer capital) delay or accelerate this transition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third sort of produce — industry efficacy limited or uncertain: prices variable with accidents
rubrics_metrics.description: For commodities where the power of industry to augment quantity is limited or uncertain, their real price tends to rise with improvement but may sometimes fall, remain the same, or rise more or less depending on accidents that affect industry's success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These goods' supply responses are irregular and contingent (e.g., appendages to other products like wool/hides tied to the number of cattle). Variation arises from both production uncertainties and changes in associated production (stock levels, agricultural practices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent and nature of markets shape price response to improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a commodity's price rises with domestic improvement depends on the geographic extent of its market: goods with markets confined to the producing country (butcher's meat) will be more affected by local improvement than goods with international markets (wool, raw hides), which may see less relative price change from one country's improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a product is easily transportable and traded internationally, improvement in one country has limited effect on its world market price; local prices for non-tradables or locally consumed goods rise more sharply with local improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete cultivation requires prices high enough to cover good-corn-land rent and ordinary profits
rubrics_metrics.description: No country's lands can be completely cultivated until the price of each produce that must be raised upon them has risen enough to (1) pay the rent of good corn land (which regulates rents) and (2) pay the labour and expense of the farmer so as to replace the stock with ordinary profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus, a rise in price is a necessary precondition for investment in improvement: gain motivates improvement; if price cannot return the expense, improvement will not occur. Hence rising prices of various produce should be regarded as the necessary precursor to full cultivation and public advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perishability and storage technologies affect supply response and quality improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly perishable products (e.g., milk) are originally produced as a 'save-all' surplus and cheap; as price rises, farmers invest in better care, storage, and processing (butter, salted butter, cheese), improving quality and extending marketability, which changes supply dynamics and price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher prices justify additional labour, cleanliness, and facilities (dedicated dairy rooms); introduction of new feed/crops (clover, turnips) and methods can later increase supply and lower prices. Thus perishability interacts with technological and management changes to determine long-run prices and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence of stock increase and land improvement; time lags
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase of stock (livestock numbers) and improvement of land must proceed together; one cannot much outrun the other. Natural obstructions (tenant poverty, lack of manure, time to put land in condition) delay the transition, so complete establishment of better systems often requires long periods (decades).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy or commercial changes (e.g., Union with England) can accelerate price rises and improvements, but full diffusion through regions is gradual. Short-term observations of continued old practices often reflect these unavoidable frictions rather than mere ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decline of small occupiers reduces low-cost 'save-all' supplies, raising prices
rubrics_metrics.description: The diminution of cottagers and small landholders (who cheaply maintain poultry, pigs, and offal-fed animals) reduces the quantity of provisions produced at little or no expense, thereby raising the prices of hogs, poultry, and similar provisions earlier and faster than would otherwise occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural social changes in tenure and farm size alter supply composition; while ultimately cultivation may adjust, the interim effect is higher prices for goods formerly supplied cheaply by small occupiers.
